description: Practice prompts for GenAI interviews, keyed to interview tracks, T0-14's fifteen system-design archetypes, roles and skills. Each prompt states what a strong answer covers, the red flags, its source line and an evidence grade. Feeds the generated prep-pack page (career/08-interviewing/prep-packs.md).
basis: Prompts are quoted or closely paraphrased from what the research sessions report: T0-14 (firm table §6.2, archetypes §6.3, round formats §6.3b, the Dataford aggregate in K9), T1-03 (behavioural bank §6.2, coding formats §6.3) and T0-06 (applied-AI startup loops). The grade is that of the strongest report: B for aggregator tallies and coaching guides that T0-14 grades B (AceOffer's 112 Anthropic reports, Hello Interview); C for a single aggregator, review or listicle, and for the T1-03 synthesis; D where no prompt is reported, in which case reported_by says so and names the round description the prompt is built from. Variants named in reported_by may rest on weaker sources. Covers and red flags paraphrase the cited lines (T0-14 elicitation lists, trade-offs, Staff tells, formulas and rubrics; T1-03 STAR-AI and competencies C1–C4; T0-15 and T2-01 for the D-graded tracks), and answer_source lists those lines. They are coach-authored or synthesised criteria: no firm publishes an AI interview rubric (T0-14 K10; T1-03 §6.2). Role and skill keys are editorial (D): design prompts start from each role's interview track in data/role_scores.json and add roles whose reported loops include the prompt; behavioural prompts list every role whose skills-ontology links include each competency the question tests. Aggregator counts rank reported prompts; they do not measure prevalence or pass rates (T0-14 §7.1 O1, O12).

A1.name: Multi-tenant LLM inference API / serving platform
A1.core_tension: Throughput versus latency; goodput under TTFT and TPOT SLOs
A1.staff_tell: Defines the SLO as goodput (requests per second per GPU that meet both TTFT and TPOT) rather than raw throughput, ties capacity to KV-cache maths, and specifies tenant fairness and a canary rollout with an eval gate

A2.name: GPU request-batching service
A2.staff_tell: Derives max wait from the latency budget, notes that continuous batching supersedes the timer design for generative workloads, and handles poison requests and cancellation

A3.name: Offline/async batch-inference API
A3.core_tension: Using idle capacity versus protecting online SLOs
A3.staff_tell: Treats price as a scheduling signal and batch work as the utilisation-smoothing layer for the fleet

A4.name: GPU fleet scheduling, placement, quotas/credits
A4.core_tension: Bin-packing versus fairness versus cold-start cost
A4.staff_tell: Derives placement constraints from weights plus KV memory, and notes that context length sets the concurrency ceiling

A5.name: Model-weights distribution and safe rollout
A5.core_tension: Source egress versus P2P complexity; rollback safety
A5.staff_tell: Computes the distribution time before choosing a topology

A6.name: LLM gateway / internal AI platform
A6.core_tension: Central control versus team autonomy; token-based limits
A6.staff_tell: Uses organisation-level levers: a model-change policy with eval gates, cost attribution and exception handling

A7.name: Prompt playground / prompt registry and experimentation
A7.staff_tell: Closes the loop from playground to eval to CI gate to deployment ('prompts as code')

A8.name: Enterprise RAG / permission-aware search (including multimodal documents)
A8.core_tension: Recall versus latency; ACL correctness; freshness
A8.staff_tell: Treats ACL enforcement as a retrieval-time, fail-closed invariant, evaluates retrieval (recall@k) separately from generation (faithfulness), plans the embedding-model migration, and keeps untrusted content and sensitive data from meeting in one context without egress control (the EchoLeak lesson)
A8.most_reported_at: OpenAI, Databricks, Google, Anthropic (search over 1B documents)

A9.name: ChatGPT-style assistant with context assembly and memory
A9.core_tension: Context budget versus quality; memory governance
A9.staff_tell: Explains how prompt layout drives the prefix-cache hit rate and cost, and names memory governance (what is stored, who can delete it)

A10.name: Latency-critical code completion plus coding assistant
A10.staff_tell: Pairs execution-based offline evals with online retention metrics and plans capacity for keystroke bursts

A11.name: Long-running tool-using agent platform
A11.staff_tell: Designs the blast radius first (Rule of Two), makes tools idempotent and the loop resumable, and builds the eval harness before adding agent features

A12.name: Real-time voice assistant
A12.staff_tell: States a per-stage p95 budget and overlaps stages (partial STT streamed into the LLM, sentences chunked into TTS)

A13.name: Document / multimodal ingestion and extraction at scale
A13.core_tension: Cost versus accuracy; reprocessing on model change
A13.staff_tell: Reasons in cost per correct document and versions outputs so a model or prompt change can be re-run safely

A14.name: LLM/agent evaluation platform and observability
A14.staff_tell: Sets an ownership model (the platform owns infrastructure, product teams contribute tasks) and links eval metrics to business outcomes
A14.most_reported_at: Anthropic (eval/monitoring and benchmark systems), Dataford GenAI-engineer aggregate, Staff+ listicles

A15.name: Safety, abuse and prompt-injection defence architecture
A15.staff_tell: Designs for compromise: blast-radius analysis, kill switches, an audit trail and incident response
A15.most_reported_at: Anthropic (malware analysis, safety layer), OpenAI moderation, Databricks

ai-lab-infrastructure.name: AI-lab infrastructure loop
ai-lab-infrastructure.employers: Anthropic; OpenAI infrastructure and inference teams
ai-lab-infrastructure.advice: Expect numbers early, 50–60 minute rounds and failure-mode probing; Anthropic rounds have shown a design-document review variant.

applied-ai.name: Applied-AI / AI-engineer loop
applied-ai.employers: Databricks, Google GenAI, scale-ups, Meta ML
applied-ai.advice: Drill RAG, assistant, copilot, agent, voice, extraction, eval and safety designs first.

classic-with-ai-flavour.name: Classic loop with AI flavour
classic-with-ai-flavour.employers: Meta and Google SWE, Stripe, Uber
classic-with-ai-flavour.advice: Keep classic design sharp; prepare one or two LLM-flavoured prompts (A8, A9) as insurance, and be ready to place an LLM component sensibly.

prompts.prompt: How would you build an LLM-powered enterprise search system?
prompts.reported_by: OpenAI (2026 Glassdoor review); OpenAI's PracHub ML-design pool adds low-latency RAG and an enterprise RAG assistant for internal documents
covers: Elicit corpus size and modalities, the ACL model, freshness, QPS, latency budget, citation requirement, accuracy bar and the cost of a wrong answer
ACL enforcement as a retrieval-time, fail-closed invariant: pre-filter at the index, re-check at context assembly
Hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval with rank fusion and a reranker, each stage proven on recall@k
Retrieval (recall@k) evaluated separately from generation (faithfulness)
An embedding-model migration plan; re-embedding also invalidates any semantic cache
Untrusted content and sensitive data kept from meeting in one context without egress control (the EchoLeak lesson)
red_flags: ACL post-filtering, which leaks and wastes top-k
Permissions enforced in the prompt

prompts.prompt: Design distributed search over about 1 billion documents.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (the most consistently reported design prompt, per IGotAnOffer)
covers: Vector memory = vectors × dimensions × bytes: 1B vectors at 1,024 dimensions take about 4.1 TB in fp32, 1.0 TB in int8 and 0.13 TB with product quantisation
Recall versus latency, ACL correctness and freshness
Hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval with rank fusion; a reranker only where top-k precision matters and the latency budget allows
Per-tenant indices or namespaces with an ACL pre-filter that fails closed
Re-embedding migration when the embedding model changes
red_flags: Never quantifies
ACL post-filtering, which leaks and wastes top-k

prompts.prompt: Design retrieval and reranking for coding agents.
prompts.reported_by: Databricks (one reported SWE phone screen)
covers: Hybrid retrieval with rank fusion where the corpus has identifiers, jargon or exact terms; a reranker when top-k precision matters and latency allows
Context ranked from open files, symbols and recent edits
Rerank latency versus recall; context size versus time to first token
Each retrieval stage proven on recall@k before it is added
red_flags: Surface-level technology choices with no reason or number behind them

prompts.prompt: Take-home: answer questions over about 50 documents and report recall@5 and faithfulness on a 20-question set.
prompts.reported_by: Applied-AI startup take-home (described in one write-up)
covers: Retrieval (recall@k) measured separately from generation (faithfulness)
Questions unambiguous enough that two experts would agree on pass or fail, with positive and negative cases
Hybrid BM25 plus dense retrieval and a reranker, each stage proven on recall@k before it is added
Chunk size and context prefixes
A citation and faithfulness check on every answer
red_flags: 'We'd test it with some prompts', or one uncalibrated LLM judge

prompts.prompt: Design a ChatGPT-style chat assistant at high scale, with context assembly and memory.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (chat system: 7 of 112 AceOffer reports); OpenAI (high-scale chat application); DesignGurus ('Design ChatGPT'); Meta's ML pool (LLM-based conversational assistant)
covers: Elicit DAU and concurrent streams, context length, tools, memory scope and deletion rules, moderation and multi-device sync
Cache-friendly prompt layout (static prefix first) and how it drives prefix-cache hit rate and cost
Summarisation or compaction versus a sliding window, tuned for recall first
Memory governance: write policy (supersession, contradiction), what is stored and who can delete it
Moderating a stream without blocking time to first token; SSE versus WebSocket
Server-side state versus client re-send
red_flags: Ignores streaming and latency physics (TTFT versus TPOT)
No evaluation story ('we'd test it')

prompts.prompt: Design a customer-support chatbot on a third-party LLM platform.
prompts.reported_by: Aced (formerly Exponent) list of 2026 prompts
covers: Requirements first: whether it acts or only answers, knowledge source and freshness, quality bar and the cost of a wrong answer
Context assembly: static prefix first, then memory, then trimmed history
Input moderation before generation, streamed output moderation with a small lag buffer, and a post-hoc audit pass
A golden set drawn from real failures, with production traffic sampled through the same graders
What happens when the provider is down or a model version changes behaviour
red_flags: Treats the LLM as a source of truth, with no validation
Hand-wavy safety

prompts.prompt: Design an LLM-based coding assistant, including latency-critical inline code completion.
prompts.reported_by: Meta (ML system design pool); code-completion design in coach lists
covers: Elicit the inline-completion latency budget (coach sources suggest a few hundred milliseconds), keystroke-rate bursts, code privacy and telemetry
A small model close to the user versus a large central model; prefix KV reuse as the user types
Context size versus time to first token, with context ranked from open files, symbols and recent edits
Speculative decoding, which helps most at low-to-medium QPS
Retained-after-N-seconds beats raw acceptance; execution-based offline evals paired with online retention metrics
Capacity planned for keystroke bursts
red_flags: Ignores streaming and latency physics (TTFT versus TPOT)

prompts.prompt: Design an agent system that executes tasks for users from a chat interface.
prompts.reported_by: OpenAI (Aug 2026 Glassdoor review); variants: Anthropic (an agent system that adapts to new tasks), Meta's ML pool (agentic ticket investigation), Google Cloud GenAI forward-deployed engineer loops (agentic system design)
covers: Elicit side-effect classes (read-only, reversible, irreversible), budgets (steps, tokens, wall-clock), concurrency, tenancy and human-approval policy
Blast radius first (Rule of Two): at most two of untrusted input, sensitive access and the ability to act externally, otherwise human approval
Idempotent tools and a resumable loop: an append-only event log and checkpoints
A deterministic workflow by default; an agent only where the path cannot be predetermined; sub-agents only to isolate context
Reliability over repeated trials: pass^k (0.75 per trial gives about 42% for three in a row)
The eval harness built before agent features
red_flags: An unbounded loop with no budgets
Grading only the agent's final answer

prompts.prompt: Agent-debugging round: an agent fails on a task; find out why and fix it.
prompts.reported_by: No fixed prompt reported (D): agent-debugging rounds are reported in applied-AI startup loops; the wording is this repository's
covers: Read the trace first: turns, tool calls, tokens and latency, with prompt and model versions and replay
Grade the outcome (end state), not the exact tool-call path
Several trials per task, because outputs are non-deterministic; report pass^k
Check the loop budgets and the tool router: schema validation, authorisation and idempotency keys
Turn the failure into a new eval task
red_flags: An unbounded loop with no budgets
Grading only the agent's final answer

prompts.prompt: Design a real-time AI voice system.
prompts.reported_by: PracHub software-engineer ML-design pool; Meta (ML pool); listicles
covers: Elicit the end-to-end latency target (most vendor sources say about 800 ms voice-to-voice, range about 300–1,000 ms), telephony versus WebRTC, barge-in, languages and cost per minute
A per-stage p95 budget that sums to the target: network, endpointing, STT, LLM time to first token, TTS first audio
Overlapped stages: partial STT streamed into the LLM, sentences chunked into TTS
Cascaded STT, LLM and TTS (observable, swappable) versus speech-to-speech (lower latency, less control)
Endpointing aggressiveness and interruption semantics
red_flags: Stage latencies added in sequence with no overlap (one vendor's illustrative sequential budget reaches about 1,180 ms)
Ignores streaming and latency physics (TTFT versus TPOT)

prompts.prompt: Design a document-processing pipeline that ingests heterogeneous documents for LLM use.
prompts.reported_by: Databricks; listicles add very long document summarisation and extraction with reliability targets
covers: Elicit volume per day, document types and lengths, field-level accuracy target, turnaround and human-review capacity
Cost per correct document, not per document
A small-model-first cascade with escalation versus an upfront router (savings vary 35–85% by workload)
Schema-constrained decoding versus post-validation; OCR versus a vision LLM
Single-pass long context versus chunked map-reduce (long context degrades mid-document)
Versioned outputs so a model or prompt change can be re-run safely; the batch API for non-urgent work
red_flags: Treats the LLM as a source of truth, with no validation

prompts.prompt: Design a malware-analysis system.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (Hello Interview's Anthropic Staff list)
covers: Trust boundaries first: what content is untrusted, sensitive assets, irreversible actions, tenancy and false-positive tolerance
Design for compromise: blast-radius analysis, kill switches, an audit trail and incident response
Sandboxing and egress control (a domain allowlist, no auto-rendered URLs)
Classifiers as one layer of defence in depth, measured with adaptive attacks rather than static prompt sets
False positives versus missed attacks
red_flags: 'Add guardrails' with no placement by layer
Drops classic engineering (queues, retries, idempotency) once a model appears

prompts.prompt: Design an LLM API with a safety layer.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (coaching and aggregator pages)
covers: Controls placed by layer: ingestion, retrieval, context assembly, model, tool gateway, output, egress, cost and abuse, response
Input moderated before generation; streamed output moderated with a small lag buffer; a post-hoc audit pass
Output treated as untrusted input downstream: schema validation, auto-rendering markdown and links stripped, PII and secret filters
Token-based rate limits, max output tokens and per-tenant budgets (OWASP LLM10)
False positives versus missed attacks, and the response-time overhead
red_flags: 'Tell the model to ignore malicious instructions'
A static benchmark score offered as proof that a defence works

prompts.prompt: Design safeguards for an AI system that can take actions on behalf of a user.
prompts.reported_by: Aced (formerly Exponent) list of 2026 prompts
covers: Trust-boundary analysis with the Rule of Two: untrusted input, sensitive access, ability to act externally; if all three are needed, split the agent or add approval
Assume the injection succeeds and bound the blast radius
Permissions in the tool gateway and retrieval layer, not the prompt: least privilege, scoped short-lived credentials, allowlists, human approval for irreversible actions
Egress control: a domain allowlist and proxy, no data-bearing URLs
A kill switch, audit log and incident runbook; adaptive red-team evals in CI
red_flags: Classifier-only defence: adaptive attacks bypassed 12 published defences with over 90% success in most cases
Permissions enforced in the prompt

prompts.prompt: How would you reduce hallucinations in an LLM application?
prompts.reported_by: Dataford GenAI-engineer aggregate (12 guides)
covers: Answers grounded in retrieved sources, with a citation and faithfulness check
Validators, citations and fallbacks rather than trusting the model
Retrieval (recall@k) evaluated separately from generation (faithfulness, groundedness)
Retrieve when the corpus exceeds the window, changes often or needs per-user ACLs; fine-tune for style or format, not for facts that change
Guardrails, confidence thresholds and fallbacks instead of promising 100% accuracy
red_flags: Treats the LLM as a source of truth, with no validation
Assumes a bigger context window removes the need for retrieval

prompts.prompt: What is your approach to fine-tuning? When would you fine-tune rather than prompt or retrieve?
prompts.reported_by: Dataford GenAI-engineer aggregate (12 guides)
covers: Prompt and retrieve first; fine-tune or distil when the task is narrow, stable and high-volume, a small model must hit a latency or cost target, and a golden set exists to prove parity
Fine-tune for style or format, not for facts that change; retrieve for large, changing or permissioned knowledge
The price gap between small and frontier models, quoted as ratios rather than memorised prices
A regression eval budgeted for every base-model upgrade
red_flags: Fine-tuning before showing that prompting and retrieval fail
Fine-tuning to inject facts that change

prompts.prompt: Design RAG over sensitive, fast-changing documents.
prompts.reported_by: Databricks (AI forward-deployed engineer track)
covers: Freshness: connectors and change capture feeding the ingest pipeline (parse, chunk, embed, index)
ACL metadata in every index and an ACL pre-filter that fails closed, re-checked at context assembly
Secrets kept out of prompts; per-tenant indices or namespaces
Untrusted content and sensitive data kept from meeting in one context without egress control
Retrieval quality and answer faithfulness evaluated separately
red_flags: ACL post-filtering, which leaks and wastes top-k
Permissions enforced in the prompt

prompts.prompt: Evaluate a multi-agent GenAI system in production.
prompts.reported_by: Databricks (AI forward-deployed engineer track)
covers: Trajectories and outcomes evaluated over repeated trials, with pass^k
Component evals: tool selection and argument accuracy, router accuracy
Sub-agents multiply token cost but isolate context
Production traffic sampled through the same graders, with implicit signals (regenerations, edits, abandonment, escalations)
Every incident fed back into the golden set
red_flags: Grading only the agent's final answer
No production feedback loop

prompts.prompt: Customer-style scoping round: scope a customer's GenAI use case before proposing a design.
prompts.reported_by: No reported prompt (D): scoping and customer-style rounds are reported in applied-AI startup loops; the prompt is built from T0-14's requirements step
covers: The six requirement questions: users, QPS and tokens; latency targets; whether it acts or only answers; knowledge source, freshness and permissions; quality bar and the cost of a wrong answer; constraints such as privacy, residency, vendor and on-premises
The top three requirements restated, with what is out of scope
The premise questioned: is an LLM needed, build or buy, what not to build
Latency-versus-accuracy and cost-versus-safety trade-offs translated into business terms
A staged rollout with exit criteria (MVP, then v2)
red_flags: Dismisses product requirements or acts defensively about model limitations
Opens with model architecture instead of requirements and scale

prompts.prompt: Design a surge-pricing, ETA, fraud-detection or recommendation system.
prompts.reported_by: Uber (MLE loops); Stripe (MLE: fraud and authorisation optimisation)
covers: The classic ML system design frame: data, features, training, offline metrics and deployment
Numbers only where they change the design
Where an LLM would help, placed as a sensible component
red_flags: Prepares LLM system design for an ML design round (the wrong round type)
Never quantifies

prompts.prompt: Where could ML or LLMs help in this workflow?
prompts.reported_by: Uber (Aug 2026 MLE phone screen: 15 minutes of free-form discussion after 45 minutes of coding)
covers: The premise questioned: is an LLM needed, build or buy, what not to build
An LLM component placed sensibly inside the existing system
The cost of a wrong answer, which sets the quality bar and the eval spec
Token cost per request and per month: requests × (input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price) ÷ 10^6
red_flags: Opens with model architecture or training instead of requirements and scale

prompts.prompt: Classic system design, then: now add RAG or an agent.
prompts.reported_by: Classic design rounds (the add-on pattern reported in trend pieces)
covers: Classic engineering kept once a model appears: queues, retries, idempotency
For RAG: an ACL pre-filter that fails closed, hybrid retrieval, and retrieval evaluated separately from generation
For an agent: step, token and time budgets, and a workflow unless the path cannot be predetermined
Evaluation and safety as named sections of the answer, not a closing sentence
red_flags: Drops classic engineering once a model appears
Unbounded agent loops

prompts.prompt: Design an inference API for serving LLMs.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (41 of 112 AceOffer reports); close variants in Databricks' GenAI-engineer track and Meta's ML pool
covers: Elicit tenants and priority tiers, peak RPS, input and output token distributions, streaming, TTFT p99 and TPOT targets, model sizes and a cost target
Goodput as the SLO: requests per second per GPU that meet both TTFT and TPOT
Capacity from KV-cache maths: KV bytes per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per element, then concurrency per node
Continuous batching with paged KV; colocated versus disaggregated prefill and decode
Admission control and load shedding; autoscaling on queue depth and KV utilisation, with a warm pool
Tenant fairness and a canary rollout behind an eval gate
red_flags: One request per GPU
Autoscaling on CPU
No distinction between prefill and decode

prompts.prompt: Design a token-generation service that handles about 100K requests per second.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic
covers: Traffic first: average and peak requests per second, then input and output tokens per second
Concurrent streams by Little's law (streams = arrival rate × time in system), then nodes at the per-node concurrency limit
Per-node concurrency = (HBM − weights − overhead) ÷ (KV bytes per token × context length)
Output length dominates latency: E2E = TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × inter-token latency
Goodput under TTFT and TPOT SLOs, not raw throughput
red_flags: Never quantifies
Correct arithmetic with no design consequence ('so it's a lot')

prompts.prompt: Design an end-to-end batching system for LLM inference requests (one reported variant: 100 requests should take about the same time as one).
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (among the most frequently reported design prompts; the variant comes from one report)
covers: Elicit max batch size, latency SLO, arrival rate and burstiness, input-length variance, and cancellation and timeout semantics
Static batching with a timer versus dynamic versus continuous (iteration-level) batching
Max wait derived from the latency budget (arrival rate × max wait approximates batch fill)
Length bucketing to cut padding; head-of-line blocking from long prompts
A bounded queue with backpressure, and correct demultiplexing of results under partial failure
Poison requests and cancellation
red_flags: No bound on the queue
No answer for 'one request in the batch fails'

prompts.prompt: Design an offline (asynchronous) batch-inference API.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (12 of 112 AceOffer reports); OpenAI's pool has a related long-running job: orchestrating Sora-style video generation
covers: Elicit turnaround SLA, priority relative to online traffic, result retrieval, idempotency and partial-failure semantics
Deadline-aware scheduling that fills the diurnal trough with preemptible capacity, plus checkpointing
Grouping by shared prefix to reuse the cache; cache hits inside batches are best-effort, so warm the cache first
Idempotent retries, per-item status and fairness with online traffic
Price as a scheduling signal: batch work as the fleet's utilisation-smoothing layer
red_flags: Drops classic engineering (queues, retries, idempotency) once a model appears
States provider batch-size limits without checking provider docs (secondary sources give 10,000, 50,000 or 100,000 requests)

prompts.prompt: Design GPU allocation for a cluster that serves a mix of large and small models.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (GPU cluster: 7 of 112 AceOffer reports; mixed large and small model allocation: 4)
covers: Elicit model memory footprints and tensor-parallel degrees, heterogeneous GPUs, preemption policy, per-org quotas and cold-start tolerance
Placement from weights plus KV memory; context length sets the concurrency ceiling
Dedicated pools per model versus multiplexing; tensor-parallel degree versus replica count
Warm-pool cost versus cold-start latency; reserved versus spot capacity
Bin-packing versus fairness versus cold-start cost
red_flags: Never quantifies

prompts.prompt: Design a GPU scheduling system that uses credits, with credit expiry and atomic credit transactions.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (GPU scheduling with credits); OpenAI (GPU-credit allocator, credit expiry tracking, atomic credit transactions); PracHub ML-design pool
covers: A credits ledger that is idempotent and append-only
Ledger correctness: idempotency, double-spend and reconciliation
A quota and fairness policy feeding the scheduler, with preemption of low-priority work
Placement constraints from weights plus KV memory
red_flags: Drops classic engineering (queues, retries, idempotency) once a model appears

prompts.prompt: Design large model-file distribution to a GPU fleet, with safe rollout and rollback.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (ML-model distribution: 16 of 112 AceOffer reports; large-file streaming: 2); Hello Interview's Anthropic Staff list
covers: Elicit weight size (hundreds of GB), fleet size, source bandwidth, integrity requirements, rollout and rollback policy, and time-to-ready
Distribution time before topology: T = size × nodes ÷ source egress (140 GB to 1,000 nodes from a 100 Gbps source is about 3.1 hours)
P2P swarm versus hierarchical cache versus object-store fan-out; chunk size; topology awareness
Throttling so distribution does not starve serving traffic
Hash verification, a health check and eval smoke test, and canary traffic with a rollback pointer
red_flags: Never quantifies

prompts.prompt: Design an LLM gateway and router for a multi-team AI platform.
prompts.reported_by: Listicles (no firm attribution)
covers: Elicit number of teams, providers, per-team budgets, compliance (PII), failover policy and reproducibility needs
Token-based limits, estimated before the call and reconciled after, rather than request limits
Degrade to a cheaper tier versus reject; failover on 429 or 5xx responses
Cache layers: prefix, exact, then an opt-in semantic cache per route
Pinned versus floating model versions, with a model-change policy behind eval gates and cost attribution
Central logging versus privacy
red_flags: A semantic cache on high-stakes or personalised routes

prompts.prompt: Design a prompt caching and retrieval system.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (SWE candidates, per IGotAnOffer)
covers: Cache layers in order: prefix (prompt) cache, then exact-match cache, then a semantic cache only on low-stakes, high-repeat, non-personalised routes
Prefix caching needs an exact prefix match: static content first and breakpoints at stable boundaries, with the hit rate verified
Prompt-cache economics: break-even reads per write = (w − 1) ÷ (1 − r), so one read repays a write at the multipliers quoted in October 2026
Semantic-cache hygiene: per-route thresholds, keys scoped by tenant and by prompt and model version, invalidation on embedding-model change
Semantic-cache value net of the cost of false hits
red_flags: A cache breakpoint on changing content, such as a timestamp, causing perpetual misses and repeated write charges
A semantic cache whose false-hit rate is never measured

prompts.prompt: Design a prompt playground, such as the OpenAI Playground.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (15 of 112 AceOffer reports); OpenAI (reported as a phone-screen prompt)
covers: Elicit users and scale, multi-model comparison, sharing and permissions, dataset runs and retention of completions
Content-addressed, immutable prompt versions
Streaming transport and reconnect
Fan-out cost and quotas when one prompt runs against several models
A permission model for shared prompts; retention and privacy of stored completions
The loop from playground to eval to CI gate to deployment ('prompts as code')
red_flags: Surface-level technology choices ('Kafka because Kafka')

prompts.prompt: Roofline analysis: is LLM prefill or decode compute-bound or memory-bound, and why?
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (4 of 112 AceOffer reports)
covers: Arithmetic intensity: decode at batch 1 is about 1 FLOP per byte, against an H100 ridge point of roughly 300 FLOP per byte (989 TFLOPS ÷ 3.35 TB/s)
Prefill is compute-bound and decode memory-bound, so goodput is the SLO metric
Decode ceiling: minimum time per output token = (weights + active KV) ÷ total memory bandwidth; real systems reach a fraction of it (MBU)
Prefill time ≈ 2 × parameters × input tokens ÷ (peak FLOPs × MFU)
Dense versus with-sparsity FLOPs checked before any spec-sheet number is used
red_flags: Uses the with-sparsity H100 figure (1,979 TFLOPS) as the dense BF16 number
No distinction between prefill and decode

prompts.prompt: p95 latency has jumped from about 100 ms to about 2,000 ms. Debug it.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (one report: a debugging exercise inside the design round)
covers: Segment by percentile and cohort before guessing
Split latency into queue, prefill and decode
Check batch size, KV-cache pressure and long-context outliers
Check retries and timeouts, a shift in cache-hit rate, a noisy neighbour and the diff of the last deploy
red_flags: Guessing without data
Not forming hypotheses

prompts.prompt: How would you evaluate an LLM system?
prompts.reported_by: Dataford GenAI-engineer aggregate (its most frequent question, in 19 guides)
covers: Success defined from the cost of a wrong answer, mapped from business metric to proxy to offline metric
A golden set of 20–50 tasks from real failures, unambiguous enough that two experts agree, with positive and negative cases
Capability suites kept separate from regression suites, with saturation watched
Code graders where outcomes are checkable, an LLM judge calibrated against humans elsewhere, humans to calibrate
Several trials per task, with pass^k for user-facing reliability
A CI gate on regressions, and production traffic sampled through the same graders
red_flags: 'We'd test it with some prompts'
One uncalibrated LLM judge, or a model judging its own outputs
No regression gate and no production feedback loop

prompts.prompt: Design a model evaluation and monitoring system (one variant: run evaluation benchmarks across hundreds of model variants).
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (SWE candidates, per IGotAnOffer; the benchmark variant comes from one aggregator)
covers: Elicit number of teams and agents, trial cost, grader mix, CI integration and production sampling
Sandboxed runners with a clean environment for every trial
Code versus LLM versus human graders (cost, determinism, nuance), with judge versions pinned
Trials versus cost (the batch API for offline runs); static versus rolling datasets (saturation, contamination)
Flaky-task detection, and tests for the eval itself: one reported benchmark score moved from 42% to 95% once grader bugs were fixed
Ownership: the platform owns infrastructure, product teams contribute tasks; eval metrics tied to business outcomes
red_flags: One uncalibrated LLM judge
No regression gate and no production feedback loop

prompts.prompt: Design an evaluation platform for many agent workflows.
prompts.reported_by: Staff-level listicles
covers: Trajectories and outcomes evaluated over repeated trials
The outcome (end state) graded, not the exact tool-call path
pass@k versus pass^k, and chained steps multiplying (0.98 per step over 20 steps is about 67%)
A clean, isolated environment for every trial
Trial isolation and grader calibration as the two deep dives
Ownership: the platform owns infrastructure, product teams contribute tasks
red_flags: Grading only the agent's final answer

prompts.prompt: Evaluation discussion: when would you use an LLM judge, and when human annotation?
prompts.reported_by: Google (ML-platform and GenAI design rounds, where this discussion is reported as central)
covers: Code graders first, LLM judges where needed, humans to calibrate
Judge validity: over 80% agreement with humans on MT-Bench-style tasks (2023, one benchmark), with position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias
Mitigations: swap answer order, use rubrics and references, avoid judging with the generator's model family, re-calibrate when the judge version changes
One dimension per judge, with an 'Unknown' option
Humans as the slow, costly gold standard that calibrates the rest
red_flags: A model judging its own outputs
One uncalibrated LLM judge

prompts.prompt: Give a research talk on your own work (one round of a frontier-lab loop that also has coding and values rounds).
prompts.reported_by: No reported prompt (D): built from the research-talk round in T2-01's frontier-lab loop and the research interview track (T1-03, T0-14)
covers: Research depth together with engineering depth (research taste plus the ability to build)
Your own contribution separated from the team's: 'I designed the evaluation methodology, implemented the baseline comparison…'
Measurement rigour: the evaluation methodology and the baseline comparison
Impact framing ('I shipped/scaled…') rather than academic framing ('I researched…')
red_flags: Academic framing instead of impact (a Meta veto trigger)
'We published a paper on…' with no personal contribution isolated

prompts.prompt: Scoping round: set up an AI governance programme (inventory, risk-assessment method, committee and evidence) mapped to the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001.
prompts.reported_by: No reported prompt (D): built from the governance interview track (T1-03, T0-14) and the programme work described in T0-15
covers: An AI inventory or registry: systems, owners, use cases and risk tiers
A risk-assessment method and committee operations, with one accountable programme lead and a cross-functional committee
Evidence as a by-product of delivery: Art. 12-style logs, evaluation reports, system documentation and incident records kept in the ML platform
Translation from legal text to evidence, the part of the work that is specific to compliance
Incident tracking and reporting, including the ability to halt a system
red_flags: Assumes most high-risk systems need a notified body (most Annex III points use internal control)
Treats ISO/IEC 42001 as a presumption of EU AI Act conformity (it gives none)
Dismisses guardrails as 'red tape' that slows shipping

prompts.prompt: Product or scoping round: scope a GenAI feature or pilot, from whether to use an LLM to success metrics, an evaluation rubric and exit criteria.
prompts.reported_by: No reported prompt (D): built from the product interview track (T1-03, T0-14) and the scoping round T2-01 lists for non-technical candidates
covers: The premise questioned: is an LLM needed, build or buy, what not to build; stakeholders and success metrics named
'Good' defined measurably (task success, groundedness, safety, latency, cost) and mapped from business metric to proxy to offline metric, starting from the cost of a wrong answer
A rubric whose tasks are unambiguous enough that two domain experts reach the same verdict, with positive and negative cases
Token economics: cost per request and per month from input and output tokens and prices
A staged rollout with exit criteria (MVP, then v2)
Latency-versus-accuracy and cost-versus-safety trade-offs translated into business terms
red_flags: Over-promises accuracy instead of proposing guardrails, confidence thresholds and fallbacks
Uses jargon without linking decisions to user impact

prompts.prompt: Tell me about a time your model failed catastrophically in production. How did you detect it?
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B1)
covers: Detection by alerts and monitoring, not by a customer complaint
Root-cause discipline and a postmortem artefact
Immediate remediation (rollback, fallback, routing) plus systemic prevention (alerts, eval pipelines)
What you did, not the team, ending with a metric delta and a continuous-monitoring step
red_flags: Deflects blame to teammates, data engineers or third-party model providers
Blames external factors ('the data was bad') without systematic troubleshooting

prompts.prompt: How do you explain hallucination risks to an executive demanding 100% accuracy?
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B2)
covers: Translation into business terms, with analogies and quantified impact
Guardrails, confidence thresholds and fallbacks proposed instead of over-promising
The cost of a wrong answer for this use case (a hallucination in medical summarisation versus a slightly wrong product recommendation)
red_flags: Jargon with no link to user impact
Defensive about model limitations

prompts.prompt: Describe a scenario where you chose a simple heuristic over an LLM.
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B3)
covers: Cost-awareness: knowing when not to use the expensive tool
A baseline and an eval metric that justified the choice
The constraint that decided it (latency ceiling, accuracy bar or cost cap) and the result as a metric delta
red_flags: Focuses on framework choice over data quality and metric drift

prompts.prompt: Tell me about a project where the data was severely bottlenecked, biased, or missing labels.
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B4)
covers: Proxy labels, active learning or human-in-the-loop labelling
The problem scoped to the data available
Baselines and eval metrics, with a pivot when a hypothesis failed
red_flags: Blames external factors ('the data was bad') without systematic troubleshooting

prompts.prompt: Give an example of when you caught a potential bias, privacy leak, or safety hazard in a model output.
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B5)
covers: The escalation path, including when to pause deployment and escalate to legal or trust-and-safety
A concrete action, not just 'I flagged it'
A systemic fix, with safety, fairness and privacy built into the design phase
red_flags: Dismisses guardrails as 'red tape' that slows shipping
Considers ethics only when prompted

prompts.prompt: Describe a time you shipped a feature with known model limitations. How did you communicate the risk?
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B6)
covers: Honest framing of the limitation to stakeholders
A risk-acceptance framework
A monitoring plan after launch
Cost-versus-safety trade-offs translated into business terms
red_flags: Defensive about model limitations

prompts.prompt: Tell me about the most expensive compute mistake you've made.
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B7)
covers: The cost quantified
The root cause
Systemic prevention: budget alerts, experiment tracking
Personal ownership of the mistake
red_flags: Deflects blame to teammates or providers
Describes what 'the team' did without isolating a personal contribution

prompts.prompt: How did you handle disagreement with a PM or executive about whether to ship a GenAI feature?
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B8)
covers: Data-driven pushback
A pilot or rollback proposal
The relationship preserved
Latency-versus-accuracy or cost-versus-safety trade-offs translated into business terms
red_flags: Friction with non-technical stakeholders, or dismissing product requirements
Blames the PM (a Google veto trigger)

prompts.prompt: Describe a time you had to re-architect a system mid-project because the model's behaviour changed.
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B9)
covers: Adaptability
Prompt and model versioning
An eval-gated rollout
Non-determinism treated as a first-class design constraint
red_flags: Treats ML like deterministic software

prompts.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to shut down or roll back a deployed AI feature.
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B10)
covers: Speed of response
Blast-radius analysis
Stakeholder communication
Immediate remediation plus systemic prevention (alerts, eval pipelines, postmortem artefacts)
red_flags: Deflects blame
Cannot admit mistakes (an Anthropic veto trigger)

prompts.prompt: How do you evaluate whether an LLM-based feature is actually working in production?
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B11)
covers: An offline golden set
Online sampling of production traffic through the same graders
Human calibration of the graders
A/B tests tied to business metrics
red_flags: 'We'd test it with some prompts'
No production feedback loop

prompts.prompt: Describe a system you built where the evaluation was harder than the feature itself.
prompts.reported_by: T1-03 bank (B12)
covers: Recognises that the evaluation was more complex than the feature
Grader design
Contamination management
Tests for the eval itself (one reported benchmark score moved from 42% to 95% once grader bugs were fixed)
red_flags: One uncalibrated LLM judge, or a model judging its own outputs

prompts.prompt: Classic algorithmic coding round, with no AI assistant: solve a data-structures and algorithms problem.
prompts.reported_by: Google, Meta (still the primary format), Stripe and many others
covers: The approach communicated before coding
Standard data structures plus optimisation
Edge cases tested
Time and space complexity stated
red_flags: Jumping to code without framing
Silent coding
Not testing

prompts.prompt: AI-enabled coding round: solve the task with an AI assistant in the editor.
prompts.reported_by: Meta (spring 2026, early signal)
covers: Orient first: confirm the input, the output and the SLA before writing code (about the first 10% of the clock)
Decide what to delegate and what to own, and say it aloud ('the assistant scaffolds the data loader while I design the retrieval loop')
Audit AI output line by line; catching a hallucination scores higher than writing clean code from scratch
Harden at the end: time and space complexity, and failure modes such as a downstream API timeout
red_flags: 'Vibe coding': pasting giant prompts and accepting unverified output
Silent AI interaction
Cannot explain AI-generated code

prompts.prompt: Design-document review: critique a pre-written system design and prioritise your findings.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic (3 reports, first observed April 2026); Aced says the format has come up for staff-level engineers and engineering leaders
covers: What the round tests: missing requirements, capacity assumptions, failure modes, rollout and alternatives
A checklist covering requirements, numbers, failure modes, migration, observability, security and alternatives rejected
A time-boxed read, then findings ordered by severity
red_flags: Surface-level comments ('could use more comments')
Missing the structural issues

prompts.prompt: Hybrid coding and design: build a service that calls an external ride API, then make it work at 100x volume.
prompts.reported_by: Anthropic
covers: A traffic estimate first: average and peak requests per second at 100x
Downstream failure handling: timeouts, retries and idempotency
Backpressure: a bounded queue that sheds load or returns 429 with retry-after, rather than unbounded queueing
Time and space complexity of the core logic
red_flags: Drops classic engineering (queues, retries, idempotency)
Over-engineers beyond the stated scale
